title: GeoMind: Dancing with Geometric Brain Rhythm on Symmetric Positive Definite Manifolds.
source: PubMed · IEEE transactions on medical imaging
desc: [IEEE transactions on medical imaging] State space model (SSM) is a powerful tool in neuroscience field to characterize the dynamic nature of brain functions by elucidating the mechanism of how brain system transits between brain states and how underlying states give rise to the observed neural activities. Although tremendous efforts have been made to lend the power of deep learning and mathematical insight of SSM in various functional neuroimaging studies, current state-of-the-art methods lack a holistic view of brain state evolution as a self-organized dynamical system where each part of the brain is functionally inter-connected. Since the topological co-activation of functional fluctuations exhibits an intrinsic geometric pattern (symmetric and positive definite, SPD) on the Riemannian manifold, the call for understanding how a selective set of functional connectivities in the brain supports diverse behavior and cognition emerge a new machine learning scenario of manifold-based SSM for largescale functional neuroimages. To that end, we propose a geometric neural network of SSM, coined GeoMind, designed to uncover evolving brain states by tracking the trajectory of functional dynamics on a high-dimensional Riemannian manifold of SPD matrices. GeoMind demonstrates promising results in identifying specific brain states on task-based functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, as well as in diseases early diagnosis for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and Autism, by using resting-state fMRI. These results highlight the applicability of GeoMind in neuroscience research. To further evaluate generalizability of GeoMind, we applied GeoMind to electroencephalography (EEG) emotion datasets, outperforming competing methods and demonstrating scalability across neuroimaging modalities.

title: Large Language Model-Assisted Radiology Report Quality Assurance: Real-World Multicenter Evaluation.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] Radiology reports serve as the definitive clinical record of imaging diagnoses, with their accuracy being directly critical to patient safety. However, amid escalating workloads, manual review remains inadequate for capturing subtle errors in reports on a large scale. Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable promise in medical text processing, previous studies have predominantly been confined to radiology report text from a single imaging modality or datasets with synthetic errors. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, accuracy, and generalizability of general-purpose LLMs for quality assurance of radiology report text from multiple imaging modalities (x-ray, computed tomography [CT], and magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]), multi-anatomical regions, and multicenter clinical settings, with head-to-head comparisons conducted against radiologists of varying seniority. Radiology report texts from 3 aforementioned imaging modalities and 5 anatomical regions (head, chest, abdomen, spine, and knee) were retrospectively collected from center 1 (March 2025-May 2025) and reviewed using a clinician-annotated 5-category error taxonomy (type 1: interpretive; type 2: factual). Five LLMs (Qwen3, GPT-5.4 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Llama 4, and DeepSeek-V3.1) were benchmarked on 10,000 randomly selected reports, and the best-performing model was evaluated on the full cohort. A blinded head-to-head comparison with 3 radiologists (3-10 years of experience) used a modality-stratified, error-enriched challenge set. The radiologists subsequently rated the model-generated explanations using a 5-point Likert scale. Cross-center performance was evaluated in an independent external cohort. The same 2 senior radiologists labeled reports from both centers using the same protocol, resolving disagreements by consensus. In total, 4.6% (4431/95,582) of the reports in center 1 contained at least one confirmed text internal error. Qwen3, the selected model, achieved a report-level sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and F1-score of 0.99, 0.99, 0.90, and 0.94, respectively, with high performance across reports from the 3 imaging modalities and multiple anatomical regions and better detection of factual than interpretive errors. In the error-enriched challenge set, its error instance exact category recall exceeded that of the radiologists (0.96 vs 0.45-0.67; P<.001), with a shorter mean task completion time (5.80 vs 55.80-67.80 seconds per report

title: Virtual Follow-up Prediction of Subsolid Pulmonary Nodules: A Prospective Silent Reader Study
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology; conditions: Pulmonary Subsolid Nodules, Ground-Glass Nodules; type: OBSERVATIONAL; enrollment: 200; status: COMPLETED] The goal of this prospective, non-interventional study is to evaluate the predictive performance and potential clinical utility of an artificial intelligence (AI)-based virtual follow-up framework for incidentally detected pulmonary subsolid nodules (SSNs), including pure ground-glass and part-solid nodules. The main questions it aims to answer are: 1. Can the AI model accurately predict future CT appearances, quantitative growth characteristics, and morphological progression of pulmonary SSNs at specified follow-up intervals? 2. Does AI-assisted virtual follow-up improve radiologists' assessment of nodule progression and simulated surveillance management decisions compared with assessment without AI assistance? Researchers will compare radiologists' assessments with and without access to AI-generated future CT images and quantitative predictions. An additional reader evaluation will examine whether generated future images provide incremental value beyond quantitative predictions alone. Participants will undergo clinically indicated CT examinations and receive routine care according to standard clinical practice. The research team will: * Collect previously acquired CT images and clinical information. * Generate and lock AI predictions before the corresponding follow-up CT examinations occur. * Obtain and lock radiologists' assessments and simulated management recommendations before actual follow-up outcomes become available. * Compare predicted nodule progression with observed follow-up CT findings. AI predictions and research-related reader assessments will not be disclosed to treating clinicians or used to alter patients' actual surveillance or treatment decisions.

title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces
desc: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant scattering has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models. We leverage a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model to analyze polarized resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) from molecular thin films. This new analysis establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states as a function of depth with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit via locking energy and polarization through the optical model. From our analysis, we discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from the interface, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics and contradicting hypotheses of substrate patterning. This nondestructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final state opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.

title: Performance of a foundation model to generate thousands of predicted outcomes across multiple use cases
desc: Background. Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models hold great promise for medical care. While many types of models have proliferated across healthcare and the life sciences, systematic, rapid generation of multi-condition predictions of diagnoses, future medical events and future clinical outcomes from a single foundation-model architecture remains rare. PhenOM(R) is a generative AI foundation model trained and validated on longitudinal medical-event data from more than 400 million patient records in the OM1 Real World Data Cloud (RWDC) and designed to complete predictive tasks for a broad array of medical diagnoses, events and clinical outcomes (collectively outcomes) at varying time intervals, currently up to five (5) years. This paper describes the implementation of PhenOM to complete a vast number of predictive tasks across clinical domains and outcomes. Methods. PhenOM was evaluated across four outcome categories (Future Risk, Screening, Care Opportunity, and Treatment Effect) in multiple domains spanning chronic disease, acute medical events, healthcare utilization, and rare and frequently undiagnosed conditions. Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Outcomes were defined within an eligible-population framework using standardized medical code sets (ICD-10, SNOMED, CPT, NDC, LOINC) unless outcomes could not be specified with an existing code. All benchmarks reported were derived from data excluded from training. Results. As of this publication, the single PhenOM model has been used to complete and validate thousands of predictive tasks covering more than 1,770 outcomes spanning most organ systems and clinical specialties, with new predictive tasks being validated each day. Overall, 80 percent of predictive tasks achieved AUROC of at least 0.70 and 30 percent achieved AUROC of at least 0.80. We present a sample of 177 of these tasks as examples that show the breadth of tasks the model can complete. Performance varied systematically by outcome and clinical domain. Conclusions. PhenOM demonstrates the ability to complete thousands of predictive tasks across clinical domains and outcomes at the individual patient level, without additional training. Outcomes include screening for undiagnosed conditions, predicting future conditions, medical events, effects of treatments, and assessing care opportunities. These can be ascertained at the individual patient and population levels. These findings

title: Large Language Models for Accurate Medical Chart Abstraction: Enabling Scalable and Secure Artificial Intelligence Deployment in Stroke
desc: Medical chart abstraction transforms unstructured clinical narratives into structured variables for research and quality monitoring. We evaluated a prompting-based large language model (LLM) framework for extracting eight clinical variables from 2,416 neurointerventional acute stroke intervention reports across three hospitals. Twenty-two instruction-tuned open-source LLMs were evaluated across architectures, model sizes, and biomedical adaptations using Quick Response and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting. Non-expert staff annotations served as the cross-model reference standard. Evaluation was restricted to report-variable pairs with a valid LLaMA3.3-70B CoT prediction and a corresponding reference label. Performance measures included extraction accuracy, inference latency, and agreement with expert adjudication. Twenty discordant cases per variable underwent review by two senior physicians and four medical students. LLaMA3.3-70B achieved the highest overall accuracy (94.8%). CoT improved performance on inference-dependent variables such as site of occlusion, while Quick Response was optimal for directly stated procedural fields. Expert adjudication showed that AI predictions were more closely aligned with expert interpretations than non-expert annotations for most variables, with intracranial angioplasty remaining a challenge. Locally deployed LLMs can support scalable clinical information extraction and retrospective stroke registry curation, with expert oversight for ambiguous cases.

title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
desc: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested, because doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies. Given a source manuscript and a target scRNA-seq dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, and reports which findings transfer and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

A clinical multimodal vision language foundation model with fine-grain explainability
desc: Despite their considerable promise, many current medical foundation models remain modality specific and lack transparent reasoning, limiting clinical adoption. To address this gap, we introduce Explainable Vision Language Foundation Model for Medicine (EVLF-FM), a multimodal vision language foundation model that combines broad diagnostic capabilities with fine-grained explainability. The development and testing of EVLF-FM encompassed more than 1.3 million total samples from 18 global datasets across 10 imaging modalities related to six clinical specialties: dermatology, hepatology, ophthalmology, pathology, pulmonology and radiology. External validation employed 13,443 independent test samples from 17 additional datasets across 10 imaging modalities. EVLF-FM supports disease diagnosis, visual question answering and pixel-level visual grounding with reasoning capabilities. In internal validation for disease diagnostics, EVLF-FM achieved the highest average accuracy, 0.895, outperforming leading generalist and specialist models. In medical visual grounding, EVLF-FM also achieved reasonable performance across nine modalities with average accuracy at 0.5 intersection over union (Acc@0.5) of 0.842. External testing further confirmed consistent zero-shot and few-shot performance, with competitive F1 scores despite a smaller model size. A hybrid training strategy combining supervised and visual reinforcement fine-tuning enables EVLF-FM to generate clinically interpretable explanations aligned with visual evidence. Human evaluation of these reasoning outputs using the S.C.O.R.E. framework yielded a high overall mean score of 4.25/5, supporting their clinical interpretability. Current limitations include the need for additional validation across diverse healthcare settings. Prospective clinical studies are required to evaluate the safety, effectiveness and clinical utility of EVLF-FM before routine clinical deployment.

title: AI-Enabled Patient Profiling for Personalized Nursing Care and Health Support: Scoping Review.
source: PubMed · Journal of medical Internet research
desc: [Journal of medical Internet research] AI-enabled patient profiling has been proposed to organize heterogeneous patient data and support personalized nursing care and health support. Given the growing use of AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), digital phenotyping, and digital twins in health care, it is important to clarify how patient profiling has been conceptualized, applied, and evaluated in nursing-relevant contexts. This scoping review aimed to examine and report the available evidence on AI-enabled patient profiling for personalized nursing care and health support. This scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews). Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to May 18, 2026, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, PubMed, CINAHL, Web of Science, and Embase. Eligible studies used AI or computational intelligence methods to construct, classify, apply, validate, or evaluate patient profiles or related patient representations relevant to personalized nursing care or health support. Two reviewers independently screened records, assessed full texts, and charted data using a predefined form. Data were synthesized descriptively and narratively using an input-process-output framework. A total of 61 studies were included. AI-enabled patient profiling was represented through patient profiles, patient or user personas, digital phenotypes, patient segments, clinical subtypes, digital twins, and LLM-enabled personalization. Included studies used diverse data sources, including electronic health records, nursing records, patient-reported outcomes, questionnaires, mobile app data, wearable and sensor data, engagement logs, and textual or conversational data. Common AI approaches included machine learning, clustering, deep learning, natural language processing, recommender systems, knowledge graphs, digital twin modeling, and LLMs. Applications focused on personalized education, self-management support, rehabilitation, chronic disease management, remote monitoring, decision support, follow-up care, and shared decision-making. title: Sequential Digital Intervention to Increase Influenza Vaccination in Patients With Heart Failure
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Heart Health Research Center; conditions: Heart Failure, Influenza Vaccination; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 588; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] Influenza vaccination is an important preventive measure for patients with heart failure (HF), but vaccination uptake remains low in China. Although previous studies have demonstrated the benefits of actively promoting influenza vaccination, scalable strategies to improve vaccination uptake among patients with HF after hospital discharge remain insufficiently evaluated. The PANDA-BOOST trial is a prospective, pragmatic, open-label, two-stage sequential randomized clinical trial involving participants previously enrolled in the PANDA II trial. The study aims to evaluate whether sequential digital interventions using artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted telephone calls and short message service (SMS) reminders improve influenza vaccination uptake compared with a single routine vaccination recommendation. After an initial AI-assisted telephone call providing a standardized influenza vaccination recommendation, eligible unvaccinated participants will be randomized in a 1:2 ratio to a routine recommendation group or a sequential digital intervention group. Participants in the sequential intervention group will receive additional AI-assisted telephone calls approximately 14 and 28 days after the initial call. Those who remain unvaccinated and meet eligibility criteria at the third call will undergo a second randomization in a 1:1:1 ratio to no additional SMS, gain-framed SMS, or loss-framed SMS. The primary outcome is influenza vaccination uptake within two months after the first-stage randomization.

title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
desc: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

title: TRACER, a time-to-event EHR foundation model for disease detection across health systems
desc: Foundation models trained on longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) can predict clinical diagnoses years in the future, making them a potential tool for disease screening. We developed TRACER (Temporal Risk Assessment with Clinical EHR Representations), a decoder-based foundation model pretrained on data from over 4.5 million patients from four health systems, and evaluated it on 16 incident diseases at 1-, 2-, and 5-year horizons in more than 2 million patients from two health systems excluded from model development. In contrast to typical evaluations that focus on global metrics (e.g., AUROC), we measured performance at the low false-positive rates that are realistic for screening. We found that TRACER retained its discrimination in external health systems, and at 95% specificity, the patients it flagged were up to eight times more likely to be diagnosed within a year than unselected patients. Evaluating at this operating point also revealed what global metrics alone did not: detection and false-alert burden varied across diseases and health systems, even when discrimination appeared stable. Our results illustrate the potential of foundation models for screening and underscore the need for evaluation in health systems excluded from development to assess disease detection and false-alert burden at levels appropriate for intended clinical use.}

title: DiaBench: A Benchmarking Framework to Evaluate the Performance of LLMs in T2D Patient Education
desc: Background Effective type 2 diabetes (T2D) education improves patient outcomes, but clinician time constraints limit what can be covered during encounters. Large language models (LLMs) offer a scalable way to answer patient questions, yet their accuracy and reliability in T2D education across health literacy levels remain poorly characterized. Methods We developed DiaBench, a standardized benchmarking framework built from 96 question-and-answer pairs collected by clinicians from representative real-world patient encounters. GPT-5 transformed each pair into multiple-choice questions (MCQs) under three configurations (1-3) simulating different question formats and levels of user background. A five-member panel of certified diabetes care and education specialists (CDCESs), medical doctors (MDs), and endocrinologists validated the transformations, rating question rephrasing, answer rephrasing, and answer correctness. We then evaluated seven LLMs (GPT-51, Gemini-2.5-Flash2, Cohere Command3, Llama-44, DeepSeek-R15, Perplexity Sonar6, Mistral-Large-2.07) for accuracy and self-consistency across three runs. Results (i) Expert validation showed a consensus over MCQ transformation. For configuration 1, 98.1% (SD 0.01) of rephrased answers were appropriate, 98.1% (SD 0.01) of MCQ answers were correct, and 95.0% (SD 0.05) of rephrased questions were appropriate; corresponding values for configuration 2 were 96.3% (SD 0.05), 97.5% (SD 0.02), and 89.8% (SD 0.14). (ii) across benchmarking for configurations 1 and 2, most models achieved high accuracy ([≥]95%), but Mistral-Large-2.0, Llama 4, and Perplexity Sonar showed substantially lower self-consistency (60.4%-91.7%) than other models ([≥]95%). All models degraded in both accuracy and self-consistency on configuration 3. Conclusions DiaBench quantitatively differentiates LLM capability in T2D patient education, with Gemini, GPT-5, and DeepSeek-R1 performing strongly and other models suboptimally. DiaBench provides a transferable platform for evaluating existing and newly developed LLMs, addressing the need for standardized benchmarking before clinical deployment of LLM-based systems in patient education.

title: Verifiable Agentic Science on Public Infrastructure
desc: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents are transforming the practice of science. Across every discipline, researchers are handing data analysis to coding agents that can design and execute complex studies from a single prompt. Yet this revolution carries a threat. When agents improvise in local environments, they leave no verifiable record, ultimately risking a wave of irreproducible science. Solving this crisis requires moving agentic science onto public infrastructure where every action leaves an examinable trail. Here we connect autonomous coding agents to shared computing resources, turning ephemeral prompts into auditable scientific records. After showing that 30 unguided local agents splinter into 18 incompatible pipelines on the same dataset, we conduct an agentic reproduction and discovery study on a large scale---reproducing a large, diverse array of studies with every workflow, history, and intermediate dataset publicly accessible. This complete provenance trail exposes unstated modeling choices, reference mismatches, and subsampled tutorial inputs in published studies, and establishes a new foundation where human scientists can understand, steer, and trust AI-driven discovery.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: From Predictive Models to Generative, Multimodal, and Agentic AI.
desc: [Bioengineering (Basel, Switzerland)] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across the diagnostic pathway, from screening and disease detection to differential diagnosis, prognostic stratification, and treatment-response assessment. This narrative review examines predictive, generative, multi-modal, and agentic AI through a diagnostic-science lens and evaluates the evidence required for translation into clinical practice. Predictive models can identify complex patterns in images, physiological signals, laboratory data, and electronic health records, but high retrospective accuracy does not establish diagnostic utility. Clinical validity and utility depend on the intended use, target population, disease spectrum and prevalence, reference standard, operating threshold, calibration, and the consequences of false-positive and false-negative results. Generative AI may support problem representation, differential diagnosis, information synthesis, and documentation, yet fluent outputs can omit critical alternatives, amplify false premises, or convey unjustified certainty. Multimodal systems may better reflect clinical reasoning by integrating imaging, text, signals, pathology, and molecular data, but they must demonstrate incremental value over the best single-modality test and remain robust to missing data. Agentic systems can coordinate evidence retrieval, test selection, and sequential workflows, thereby increasing the need for bounded permissions, auditability, error recovery, and human escalation. Across all paradigms, a credible pathway to diagnostic implementation requires independent external and prospective validation, representative consecutive patients, subgroup analysis, workflow and human-AI evaluation, clinical impact studies, and post-deployment surveillance. The field should therefore be judged not by model capability alone, but by whether AI measurably improves diagnostic yield, timeliness, safety, equity, and patient-relevant outcomes in real care settings.

title: Artificial Intelligence Software (Prostate Intelligence) for Detecting Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer on MRI
desc: [Newly registered clinical trial, no results yet; sponsor: Fondazione Policlinico Universitario Agostino Gemelli IRCCS; conditions: Prostate Cancer; type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: NA; enrollment: 226; status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING] The goal of this study is to learn how accurately an artificial intelligence (AI) software called Prostate Intelligence (Pi) detects clinically significant prostate cancer on prostate MRI in adults with a prostate gland who are referred for MRI because prostate cancer is suspected. The main question it aims to answer is: \- How sensitive and specific is Pi, used on its own, in detecting clinically significant prostate cancer (Gleason grade 3+4 or higher) at the patient level? Researchers will also compare Pi, the radiologist alone, and the radiologist assisted by Pi, to see whether AI assistance changes cancer detection. Participants will: * Undergo prostate MRI as part of their usual clinical care. Each MRI is first read by a radiologist without the AI result; the Pi report is then shown to the radiologist, who produces a final combined report. * Undergo targeted prostate biopsy (up to two lesions) if the MRI is suspicious, as in routine practice. Areas flagged only by Pi may also be biopsied. * If not biopsied, be followed for 12 months after MRI with PSA tests at 6 and 12 months and clinical assessment, to confirm the absence of clinically significant cancer. About 226 participants will be enrolled at two Italian centres (Fondazione Policlinico Universitario A. Gemelli IRCCS, Rome, and IRCCS Ospedale San Raffaele, Milan).

title: CellTrack-Bench: Microscopic Cell Tracking Benchmark for Vision-Language Models
desc: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
